title: The Reactivity Series

# The Reactivity Series

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- State the order of metals in the reactivity series
- Explain what makes a metal reactive
- Predict reactions based on the reactivity series
- Describe how the reactivity series was determined

## Introduction

Metals vary greatly in how reactive they are. Some metals, like potassium, react violently with water, while others, like gold, barely react at all. The **reactivity series** ranks metals in order of their reactivity.

## Key Concepts

### The Reactivity Series

| Metal | Symbol | Reactivity |
|-------|--------|------------|
| Potassium | K | Most reactive |
| Sodium | Na | ↑ |
| Lithium | Li | \| |
| Calcium | Ca | \| |
| Magnesium | Mg | \| |
| Aluminium | Al | \| |
| (Carbon) | (C) | \| |
| Zinc | Zn | \| |
| Iron | Fe | \| |
| (Hydrogen) | (H) | \| |
| Copper | Cu | \| |
| Silver | Ag | \| |
| Gold | Au | ↓ |
| Platinum | Pt | Least reactive |

**Memory aid:** **P**lease **S**top **L**icking **C**a**M**els **A**nd **Z**ebras **I**n **H**ot **C**ountries **S**igned **G**eneral **P**latypus

(Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points, though they are non-metals)

### What Makes a Metal Reactive?

**Reactive metals:**
- Lose electrons easily
- Form positive ions readily
- Have low ionisation energy
- Electrons are further from nucleus (larger atoms)

**Less reactive metals:**
- Hold onto electrons more tightly
- Don't form ions easily
- Have higher ionisation energy

### Groups in the Reactivity Series

**Very reactive metals (K, Na, Li, Ca):**
- React vigorously with cold water
- React explosively with acids
- Stored under oil to prevent reaction with air/water

**Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Al, Zn, Fe):**
- React slowly with cold water (or not at all)
- React well with steam
- React with acids
- Found as compounds in ores

**Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au, Pt):**
- Don't react with water
- Don't react with most acids
- Often found as pure metals in nature
- Used in jewellery and coins

### How the Reactivity Series is Determined

**Reactions with water:**
[DIAGRAM: Test tubes showing different metals in water - vigorous bubbling for Na, slow for Mg, none for Cu]

**Reactions with dilute acid:**
- Compare speed of hydrogen production
- More reactive metals produce hydrogen faster

**Displacement reactions:**
- A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one
- Used to compare metals directly

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Put these metals in order of reactivity: Iron, Magnesium, Copper, Sodium

**Solution:**
From the reactivity series:
Sodium > Magnesium > Iron > Copper

**Answer:** Sodium (most reactive), Magnesium, Iron, Copper (least reactive)

---

**Example 2:** Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.

**Solution:**
- Potassium has more electron shells than sodium
- The outer electron is further from the nucleus
- There is more shielding from inner electrons
- The outer electron is lost more easily
- Therefore potassium is more reactive

---

**Example 3:** Predict whether zinc will react with copper sulfate solution.

**Solution:**
- Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series
- Zinc is more reactive than copper
- A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive one
- Therefore, zinc WILL react with copper sulfate

$$\text{Zn} + \text{CuSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{Cu}$$

---

**Example 4:** Will copper react with zinc sulfate solution? Explain.

**Solution:**
- Copper is below zinc in the reactivity series
- Copper is less reactive than zinc
- A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one
- Therefore, copper will NOT react with zinc sulfate
- No reaction occurs

## Reactions Summary

| Metal | Reaction with water | Reaction with dilute acid |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| K, Na | Violent, floats, may ignite | Too dangerous |
| Li | Vigorous, floats | Too dangerous |
| Ca | Steady bubbles, sinks | Very vigorous |
| Mg | Very slow (reacts with steam) | Vigorous |
| Al | None (oxide layer) | Moderate (once oxide removed) |
| Zn | None (reacts with steam) | Moderate |
| Fe | None (reacts with steam) | Slow |
| Cu | None | None (with dilute HCl/H₂SO₄) |
| Ag, Au | None | None |

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that aluminium appears unreactive due to its oxide layer
- **Correct:** Aluminium is actually quite reactive but its oxide layer protects it

- **Mistake:** Thinking all metals react with acids
- **Correct:** Unreactive metals like copper, silver, and gold don't react with dilute acids

- **Mistake:** Confusing the order of metals
- **Correct:** Learn a mnemonic and practice regularly

## Practice Questions

1. Write the reactivity series for these metals in order from most to least reactive: Fe, Mg, Cu, Na, Zn (2 marks)

2. Explain why calcium is more reactive than magnesium. (3 marks)

3. Predict whether magnesium will react with iron(II) sulfate solution. Explain your answer and write an equation if a reaction occurs. (4 marks)

4. A student adds a piece of copper to silver nitrate solution. Describe and explain what happens. (4 marks)

5. Explain why gold is often found as a pure metal in nature, while iron is found in ores as iron oxide. (3 marks)

6. Why is aluminium used for aircraft bodies even though it is quite reactive? (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Reactivity series | A list of metals in order of their reactivity |
| Ionisation energy | The energy needed to remove an electron from an atom |
| Displacement | When a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one |
| Ore | A rock containing enough metal compound to make extraction worthwhile |
| Native metal | A metal found naturally in its pure form |

## Summary

- The **reactivity series** lists metals in order of reactivity
- Most reactive: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pt (least)
- Reactive metals lose electrons easily and form ions readily
- More reactive metals:
  - React with cold water
  - React vigorously with acids
  - Are found as compounds (ores)
- Less reactive metals:
  - Don't react with water or dilute acids
  - May be found as pure metals
- The series is used to predict displacement reactions
